title: Combined Emergency Medicine Anesthesiology Residency Program
level: Clinical physician residency (distinct combined EM–anesthesiology programme; independent-study derivative)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: For this independent course: prior study of anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and acute-care terminology; ability to read clinical guidelines critically.
Recommended learner level: senior health-professions student, resident, fellow, or clinician working with direct faculty supervision.
Not a prerequisite waiver for Johns Hopkins admission. Johns Hopkins uses ResidencyCAS/NRMP for PGY-1 positions and publishes its own application requirements.
No learner may use this course as authorization for intubation, sedation, regional anesthesia, EMS command, prescribing, or unsupervised patient care.
objectives: Explain the identity and 60-month structure of the named combined programme without conflating it with self-study.
Integrate airway, ventilation, resuscitation, shock, trauma, perioperative, pediatric/obstetric, pain, EMS, and handoff reasoning in fictional cases.
Use current public AHA, ASA, SCCM, CDC, ACGME, ABEM, and ABA sources with explicit scope limits.
Navigate ABEM and ABA public board frameworks without reproducing protected exam content.
Recognize when local protocol, direct supervision, or specialty consultation is required.

unitMap.text: Programme identity, dual-specialty scope, and educational limits
Airway assessment and strategy across ED and perioperative settings
Oxygenation, ventilation, monitoring, and airway confirmation
Peri-intubation physiology and hemodynamic risk
Cardiac arrest, arrhythmia, and post-arrest systems
Shock, sepsis, hemorrhage, and critical-care transition
Trauma and emergency-anesthesia interfaces
Pediatric and obstetric emergency–anesthesia intersections
Pre-op, NORA, PACU, ICU, and ED handoffs
Acute pain, regional-analgesia concepts, and opioid-safety limits
Cardiac, neuroanesthesia, and high-risk physiology
EMS, disaster medicine, and resource-aware acute care
Quality improvement, professionalism, evidence appraisal, and human factors
Board-source navigation and integrated reasoning capstone

topicGaps: No public, observed-duration Johns Hopkins combined-programme clinical didactic lecture series was verified. The added clinical recordings are external society/ILCOR/OpenAnesthesia teaching, not Hopkins curriculum.

The verified video floor is met numerically, but topic coverage is uneven: the long-form ledger concentrates on resuscitation and obstetric anesthesia. It does not constitute a balanced 36-hour combined EM–anesthesia sequence.

Public sources conflict or are temporally incomplete: Johns Hopkins application information describes first/final years as all Emergency Medicine, while the current ACGME combined curricular document requires equal time in both specialties in each academic year; no public current block diagram reconciles this.

Insufficient public full-length video instruction remains for adult emergency difficult-airway practice, adult trauma systems, adult cardiac/neuroanesthesia beyond obstetric intersections, current adult critical-care/ventilation, EMS command/disaster operations, and cross-specialty perioperative transitions. Use current primary guidance and supervised institutional teaching.
No clinical rotations, case logs, procedure simulation, direct observation, feedback, or credentialing can be supplied by this course; the public video hour floor does not close these practice gaps.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician residency (distinct combined EM–anesthesiology programme; independent-study derivative)
medical.boardStatus: Johns Hopkins’ directory labels the programme ACGME Accredited. ABA and ABEM jointly approve combined training; completion supports separate initial-certification processes in Emergency Medicine and Anesthesiology. No separate “Combined Emergency Medicine–Anesthesiology” board certificate is identified in the reviewed board sources.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Only satisfactory completion of 60 months of approved combined training, verified by the designated programme leaders, meets the joint training criterion. ABEM eligibility begins after graduation, programme-director verification, and ABEM licence verification; ABA requires its own BASIC, ADVANCED, and APPLIED pathway. This course neither supplies training credit nor eligibility, certification, licensure, privileges, or examination access.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Combined Emergency Medicine Anesthesiology Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Directory: ACGME Accredited, five years. The programme page reports two residents/year and five years; application page says first and final years are all Emergency Medicine. It does not expose a complete current block diagram or a public didactic lecture series with durations.

programmeSourceScope.classification: Actual separate, named combined clinical physician-residency programme—not a generic directory category.
programmeSourceScope.scope: Exactly one official institutional offering is included: Johns Hopkins. No Harvard, Emory, nuclear medicine, radiology, imaging-informatics, adult/pediatric fellowship, or research-only track is silently merged into this entry.
programmeSourceScope.overlapsAndVariants: ABA’s current combined-program list names Johns Hopkins University under Emergency Medicine and Anesthesiology. The combination includes two existing specialties; it does not create a third certification. No second official Johns Hopkins institutional variant was found in the reviewed sources.
programmeSourceScope.rotationTransparency: Public sources conflict or are temporally incomplete: Johns Hopkins’ application page says first/final years are all EM, while the current ACGME combined curricular document says time in the two specialties must be allocated equally each academic year. No public current block schedule reconciles this; none is invented here.

sourceCaveats: Programme, ACGME, and board documents have different purposes. A public programme description is not a complete curriculum or proof of an individual’s competence.
The possible difference between the Johns Hopkins application-page year description and the 2025 ACGME combined curricular document is flagged rather than reconciled by inference.
The AHA 2025, ASA 2022, SSC 2026, and CDC 2022 sources were checked on the stated date; guidance and local policy can change.

Observed video durations are deduplicated by Vimeo video ID and come from public oEmbed metadata plus a public-player HTTP check. The videos are foundation orientations, not specialty clinical lectures.
Free viewing does not grant rehosting rights. TCIA and Radiopaedia images are linked only with their stated license/citation conditions.

topicGaps: No public, observed-duration Johns Hopkins combined-programme clinical didactic lecture series was verified. The added clinical recordings are external society/ILCOR/OpenAnesthesia teaching, not Hopkins curriculum.

The verified video floor is met numerically, but topic coverage is uneven: the long-form ledger concentrates on resuscitation and obstetric anesthesia. It does not constitute a balanced 36-hour combined EM–anesthesia sequence.

Public sources conflict or are temporally incomplete: Johns Hopkins application information describes first/final years as all Emergency Medicine, while the current ACGME combined curricular document requires equal time in both specialties in each academic year; no public current block diagram reconciles this.

Insufficient public full-length video instruction remains for adult emergency difficult-airway practice, adult trauma systems, adult cardiac/neuroanesthesia beyond obstetric intersections, current adult critical-care/ventilation, EMS command/disaster operations, and cross-specialty perioperative transitions. Use current primary guidance and supervised institutional teaching.
No clinical rotations, case logs, procedure simulation, direct observation, feedback, or credentialing can be supplied by this course; the public video hour floor does not close these practice gaps.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has predictors of difficult intubation, anticipated difficult mask/supraglottic ventilation, and high aspiration risk. Which statement best matches the ASA guideline?

options.text: Proceed with repeated anesthetized attempts because a backup device is available.
Consider awake intubation when difficult intubation is expected and difficult ventilation or increased aspiration risk is present.
Avoid supplemental oxygen during airway management.
Defer planning until the first attempt fails.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASA says awake intubation should be considered when difficult intubation is suspected plus difficult ventilation, aspiration risk, inability to tolerate brief apnea, or difficult invasive rescue. It also emphasizes preparation, oxygenation, and limiting attempts. This is a reasoning question, not a procedure instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a fictional adult cardiac arrest, which 2025 AHA principle best governs advanced-airway timing?

options.text: It must precede defibrillation.
Choice and timing should weigh clinician skill and patient factors against interruption of high-quality chest compressions.
Endotracheal intubation is the only acceptable strategy.
Capnography is never useful before ROSC.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AHA notes that basic or advanced airway strategies may be considered. Risks of interruption, malposition, and hyperventilation must be weighed; in shockable rhythms CPR and defibrillation remain central.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about waveform capnography in fictional cardiac arrest is most accurate?

options.text: A low ETCO2 proves a misplaced tube.
It can confirm an endotracheal tube during arrest, but sensitivity falls after prolonged arrest and ETCO2 has multiple determinants.
It is independent of compression quality and ventilation.
It alone should determine termination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline reports strong specificity for confirming ETT position in arrest, lower sensitivity after prolonged arrest, and multiple factors affecting ETCO2. One value must not be overinterpreted.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a fictional adult with sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, which SSC 2026 statement is paired correctly with its qualifier?

options.text: Never give fluid before a central line.
Give at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours, with frequent reassessment and patient-context attention.
Use qSOFA as the preferred single in-hospital screen.
Delay antimicrobials until definitive microbiology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SSC 2026 suggests at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours while stressing reassessment and avoidance of under/over-resuscitation. It recommends NEWS/NEWS2/MEWS/SIRS rather than qSOFA alone for in-hospital screening.
practiceQuestions.domain: Shock/sepsis; ABEM infection/cardiovascular; ABA critical care

practiceQuestions.stem: What minimum duration is required for dual-certification eligibility in the published ABEM–ABA combined-training guideline?

options.text: 36 months at one hospital.
48 months if BASIC is passed.
60 months of satisfactory combined education verified by both programmes’ designated leaders.
60 months plus automatic certification without examinations.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The joint guideline requires 60 months with verification by both programme leaders. Completion meets training criteria to enter each board process; it does not award either certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which set of experiences is explicitly listed in the current ACGME combined curricular document?

options.text: Two months each of obstetric, pediatric, neuro-, and cardiothoracic anesthesiology; three months pain; 0.5 month each PACU, pre-op, NORA.
A mandatory two-year research block and no critical care.
Only ED rotations because anesthesia competency is assumed.
One month of every anesthesia subspecialty without limits.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current document lists those requirements plus EM, critical-care, pediatric, and EMS experiences. It is a minimum standard, not a published Johns Hopkins block schedule.

practiceQuestions.stem: When does ABEM board eligibility begin for a graduate of an ABEM-approved combined programme, assuming the licence policy is met?

options.text: First day of PGY-1.
At residency application.
After graduation once the program director verifies completed training.
Only after ABA APPLIED.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM says eligibility begins after graduation when the programme director verifies completed training and ABEM verifies medical-licence status. Watching this course cannot create eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which sequence accurately describes ABA’s publicly stated initial-exam pathway?

options.text: APPLIED before BASIC, then ADVANCED after fellowship.
BASIC at end of CA-1; ADVANCED after residency and BASIC; APPLIED after ADVANCED.
ADVANCED in medical school; BASIC after APPLIED.
One combined EM–anesthesia written exam replaces all ABA exams.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA describes BASIC at the end of CA-1, ADVANCED after residency and BASIC, and APPLIED after ADVANCED. The combined pathway does not create a combined ABA exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: ABEM says the QE is based on which public framework, and what is the stated Procedures & Skills percentage?

options.text: EM Model; 8%.
ABA ADVANCED Blueprint; 20%.
ACGME milestones; 3%.
A proprietary combined-program bank; 50%.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM describes approximately 305 single-best-answer questions based on the EM Model and lists Procedures & Skills at 8%. The framework is useful for topic planning, not for reconstructing secure content.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly respects the scope of the CDC 2022 opioid-pain guideline?

options.text: It is an inflexible law replacing clinical judgment.
It is for outpatients aged 18+ with acute, subacute, or chronic pain and excludes cancer-related pain, palliative care, and end-of-life care.
It gives a universal intraoperative protocol.
It only concerns opioid-use-disorder treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC describes outpatient adult pain-care recommendations and explicit exclusions. It is not a replacement for individualized judgment or FDA labeling.

title: Pain Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Intended educational level: advanced health-professions learners and physicians who already understand general anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, evidence appraisal, and basic history/examination principles.

No learner credential is created or verified by this course. Access does not authorize patient assessment, prescribing, sedation, imaging interpretation, procedures, device management, or use of controlled substances.
For the fellowship itself, Johns Hopkins publishes its own application and legal/licensure requirements; those are not prerequisites satisfied by this independent course.
objectives: Use current IASP terminology and a biopsychosocial, function-centered formulation of pain.
Build a safe, differential-based assessment and recognize red-flag, urgent, and specialty-referral boundaries.
Compare multimodal pharmacologic, behavioral, rehabilitation, integrative, and procedural concepts by benefit, harm, evidence, and patient goals.
Explain opioid and gabapentinoid safety principles without substituting for individualized prescribing supervision.
Map acute, musculoskeletal, neuropathic, cancer, visceral, headache/orofacial, and special-population domains to the public ABA blueprint.
Recognize that interventions, sedation, imaging, and implanted-device care require supervised clinical training, local policy, and credentialing.
Use direct primary sources to check certification, guideline scope, labeling, image licensing, and evidence limitations.

units.title: Scope, language, mechanisms, and evidence
objectives: Apply the IASP definition while distinguishing pain from nociception.
Relate peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal modulation to a biopsychosocial formulation.
Appraise a pain claim using effect size, bias, and patient-important function rather than pain score alone.
topics: IASP terminology; acute/subacute/chronic framing; nociception and modulation; placebo/context effects; evidence literacy; team care
units.casePractice: Use a fictional vignette to separate a patient’s pain report, sensory findings, and presumed tissue generator; state uncertainty and functional goals.
units.assessment: Write a 250-word evidence appraisal with a PICO question and one limitation; answer Q1.

units.title: Comprehensive pain assessment, imaging, and function
objectives: Structure a history, neurologic/musculoskeletal screen, psychosocial assessment, and functional outcome review.
Recognize when imaging/electrodiagnostics answer a defined question rather than substitute for clinical reasoning.
Identify red flags and formulate escalation rather than attempt independent diagnosis.
topics: Pain descriptors; trajectories; examination; imaging and electrodiagnostics; function/disability; cultural and communication factors; outcome measures
units.casePractice: Linked-only NLM Open-i/MedPix search exercise: identify the license and source before using any image; do not rehost or infer a diagnosis from one image.
units.assessment: Submit a fictional assessment template including pain interference, sleep, mood, substance-use risk screen, and red-flag plan; answer Q2.

units.title: Pharmacotherapy and multimodal analgesia
objectives: Compare mechanism, indication logic, benefit/harms, and monitoring considerations across nonopioids, opioids, adjuvants, and topical/other agents.
Explain why drug selection is condition- and patient-specific rather than a universal ladder.
Recognize the FDA respiratory-depression warning context for gabapentinoids with opioids/CNS depressants or respiratory risk factors.
topics: Acetaminophen/NSAIDs; opioids; antidepressants/anticonvulsants; ketamine concepts; drug interactions; renal/hepatic considerations; monitoring
units.casePractice: For a fictional patient with neuropathic features and sleep disruption, compare two medication classes without writing a dose or prescription.
units.assessment: Create a benefit–risk monitoring table and answer Q4; peer-check an interaction/respiratory-risk statement.

units.title: Opioid stewardship, substance-use disorder, and safety
objectives: Explain the scope and limits of the CDC 2022 outpatient opioid guideline.
Use person-centered shared decision-making concepts when assessing benefits, risks, function, and harms.
Differentiate pain treatment, opioid use disorder treatment, and emergency care boundaries; identify when supervised referral is required.
topics: Risk assessment; PDMP/toxicology concepts; naloxone concepts; opioid agreements; tapering cautions; buprenorphine/methadone concepts; stigma; legal/regulatory context
boardDomains: ABA General: Legal and Regulatory Issues
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional patient whose pain and function worsen during an involuntary taper proposal; identify why a rigid threshold is not a substitute for individualized care.
units.assessment: Answer Q3 and draft a non-stigmatizing referral/handoff note for a fictional scenario.

units.title: Psychological, physical, rehabilitation, and integrative care
objectives: Integrate CBT/behavioral, physical rehabilitation, sleep, and self-management approaches into a goal-based plan.
Avoid falsely framing pain as “all in the head”; articulate how biological, psychological, and social factors interact.
Evaluate claims for integrative interventions and set function-focused outcomes.
topics: CBT/DBT; biofeedback; mindfulness; exercise/graded activity; sleep; OT; acupuncture; nutrition; culture, trauma, and social support
boardDomains: ABA General: Psychological, Physical, and Integrative Therapies (10%)
units.casePractice: Build a function-first, fictional interdisciplinary plan that names a patient-selected activity and a measurable follow-up outcome.
units.assessment: Reflect on language that validates pain while avoiding diagnostic overstatement; answer Q1 or Q2 as retrieval practice.

units.title: Acute, traumatic, and postoperative pain
objectives: Compare acute, subacute, and chronic pain time frames as practical rather than absolute guides.
Explain multimodal acute analgesia concepts and perioperative opioid-risk considerations.
Identify why inpatient/operative supervision and local protocols are required for regional and sedation decisions.
topics: Acute and post-surgical pain; trauma; regional concepts; multimodal analgesia; persistent postsurgical pain prevention; discharge boundaries
boardDomains: ABA Clinical States: Acute Pain, Trauma, and Procedural Pain (6.5%)
units.casePractice: Map a fictional postoperative pain transition to outpatient follow-up, noting that the CDC guideline excludes inpatient care.
units.assessment: Answer Q3 and Q5; identify three supervision-dependent tasks that cannot be learned from a recording.

units.title: Musculoskeletal and spine pain: selection, imaging, and interventions
objectives: Construct differential and conservative-care reasoning for axial and radicular pain presentations.
Describe indications, limits, complications, consent, and evidence questions for blocks, injections, and lesioning without teaching a procedure.
Explain the FDA safety context for epidural steroid injections.
topics: Low back pain; joints/bursae; facet/medial branch concepts; epidural approaches; sympathetic/peripheral blocks; fluoroscopy/ultrasound concepts; anticoagulation/infection screening
units.casePractice: Compare the clinical question, potential benefit, and complication/consent discussion for a fictional radicular-pain referral; no needle trajectory or medication/dose is produced.
units.assessment: Answer Q6 and submit a safety checklist with referral/escalation triggers.

units.title: Neuropathic pain and complex regional pain reasoning
objectives: Differentiate neuropathic descriptors/signs from a diagnosis of a specific syndrome.
Develop a differential and multidisciplinary plan for a fictional CRPS-like presentation while avoiding premature certainty.
Recognize medication, rehabilitation, psychological, and procedural considerations as complementary rather than automatically sequential.
topics: Peripheral/central neuropathic pain; allodynia/hyperalgesia; postherpetic pain; painful diabetic neuropathy; CRPS concepts; central sensitization
units.casePractice: Use a fictional limb-pain case to distinguish allodynia from a mechanism claim and state what additional assessment is needed.
units.assessment: Answer Q4 and write a differential with at least two alternatives and a red-flag escalation point.

units.title: Headache, orofacial, visceral, and chronic widespread pain
objectives: Organize common primary and secondary pain categories without treating one symptom pattern as diagnostic proof.
Recognize when headache/facial, visceral, and widespread-pain presentations need specialty or urgent evaluation.
Apply function and comorbidity assessment across diffuse pain syndromes.
topics: Migraine/headache; trigeminal/orofacial pain concepts; abdominal/pelvic/visceral pain; fibromyalgia/chronic widespread pain; autoimmune pain context
boardDomains: ABA Clinical States: Headache and Orofacial Pain (3%)
ABA Clinical States: Chronic Widespread Pain (1%)
units.casePractice: Make a fictional referral map for new persistent headache with atypical features; do not diagnose from the vignette alone.
units.assessment: Five-item short-answer taxonomy drill with source citation.

units.title: Cancer pain and palliative interfaces
objectives: Explain why cancer-related pain requires mechanism, goals-of-care, prognosis, and interdisciplinary context.
Distinguish the CDC outpatient guideline’s explicit exclusion of cancer-related pain, palliative care, and end-of-life care.
Describe consultation and symptom-support roles without issuing a patient-specific therapy order.
topics: Cancer-related pain mechanisms; bone pain; treatment-related neuropathy; opioid/nonopioid concepts; palliative/hospice coordination; intrathecal/neurolytic concepts
boardDomains: ABA Clinical States: Cancer Pain and Cancer-related Pain (6%)
ABA General: Pharmacotherapy and Procedural Treatment
units.casePractice: Use the linked Stanford CME lecture in the reading/viewing plan; write a fictional consult question that names the patient’s goal and oncology/palliative partners.
units.assessment: Answer Q3’s scope question and complete a one-page fictional interdisciplinary care-map.

units.title: Neuromodulation, targeted drug delivery, and device safety
objectives: Describe evaluation, trial, implantation, and follow-up as specialist, supervised processes rather than videos to copy.
Compare stimulation and targeted drug-delivery concepts at a high level.
Use device-specific labeling as a boundary, not as a universal indication.
topics: SCS/PNS concepts; implanted devices; targeted drug delivery; candidacy, trial response, contraindications; device labeling; adverse events
units.casePractice: Interpret the FDA’s Evoke labeling as a device-specific example and list why it cannot establish eligibility for another device or a real patient.
units.assessment: Answer Q10; produce a patient-safety boundary statement that excludes independent device or procedural action.

units.title: Special populations, ethics, systems, and synthesis
objectives: Apply equity, communication, disability, mental-health, pediatric, and substance-use considerations to a pain formulation.
Explain consent, documentation, quality improvement, and interdisciplinary handoff responsibilities.
Synthesize a fictional board-style case using uncertainty, evidence limits, and a safe escalation plan.
topics: Pediatric, geriatric, pregnancy, renal/hepatic impairment; sickle cell disease; trauma/PTSD; ethics; privacy; disability; QI; coordination
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional care-conference handoff that identifies who must provide supervised specialty care and what the learner cannot independently perform.
units.assessment: Complete the 10 original questions and a capstone source-audited fictional case synthesis.

assignment.title: Source-audited fictional interdisciplinary pain case synthesis
assignment.instructions: Create a 1,200–1,500 word synthesis for a clearly labeled fictional adult scenario. Include pain trajectory, function, psychosocial context, differential and red flags, evidence questions, nonpharmacologic/pharmacologic categories with benefit–harm/monitoring concepts, team roles, and referral/escalation boundaries. Cite at least four course primary sources. Do not give doses, write prescriptions, specify procedure technique, use a real record/image, or claim a diagnosis.
assignment.deliverable: Structured evidence-and-safety memo plus a one-page care-team map.
assignment.safetyBoundary: Educational analysis only; no patient-specific advice, procedural instruction, clinical decision, or credentialing determination.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
mapping.name: Pain Medicine Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Actual, named one-year multidisciplinary ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship—not a generic directory category. The public page reports continuous ACGME accreditation since 1994, six annual fellows, NRMP positions, and collaboration between Anesthesiology & Critical Care Medicine and Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. Publicly described clinical exposure includes outpatient/inpatient consultation, chronic nonmalignant, cancer, and pediatric pain at the Blaustein Pain Treatment Center; rotations of 1–2 weeks in Anesthesiology, Neurology/Neurosurgery, Palliative Care, PM&R, and Psychiatry; and weekly lectures, oncology/spine conferences, grand rounds, journal clubs, and multidisciplinary pain conferences. It also describes a separate optional T32 research partnership. Public page descriptions are not a complete rotation schedule, case log, or a transcript of lectures.

unitMap.text: Scope, language, mechanisms, and evidence
coveredTopics: IASP terminology; acute/subacute/chronic framing; nociception and modulation; placebo/context effects; evidence literacy; team care

unitMap.text: Comprehensive pain assessment, imaging, and function
coveredTopics: Pain descriptors; trajectories; examination; imaging and electrodiagnostics; function/disability; cultural and communication factors; outcome measures

unitMap.text: Pharmacotherapy and multimodal analgesia
coveredTopics: Acetaminophen/NSAIDs; opioids; antidepressants/anticonvulsants; ketamine concepts; drug interactions; renal/hepatic considerations; monitoring

unitMap.text: Opioid stewardship, substance-use disorder, and safety
coveredTopics: Risk assessment; PDMP/toxicology concepts; naloxone concepts; opioid agreements; tapering cautions; buprenorphine/methadone concepts; stigma; legal/regulatory context

unitMap.text: Psychological, physical, rehabilitation, and integrative care
coveredTopics: CBT/DBT; biofeedback; mindfulness; exercise/graded activity; sleep; OT; acupuncture; nutrition; culture, trauma, and social support

unitMap.text: Acute, traumatic, and postoperative pain
coveredTopics: Acute and post-surgical pain; trauma; regional concepts; multimodal analgesia; persistent postsurgical pain prevention; discharge boundaries

unitMap.text: Musculoskeletal and spine pain: selection, imaging, and interventions
coveredTopics: Low back pain; joints/bursae; facet/medial branch concepts; epidural approaches; sympathetic/peripheral blocks; fluoroscopy/ultrasound concepts; anticoagulation/infection screening

unitMap.text: Neuropathic pain and complex regional pain reasoning
coveredTopics: Peripheral/central neuropathic pain; allodynia/hyperalgesia; postherpetic pain; painful diabetic neuropathy; CRPS concepts; central sensitization

unitMap.text: Headache, orofacial, visceral, and chronic widespread pain
coveredTopics: Migraine/headache; trigeminal/orofacial pain concepts; abdominal/pelvic/visceral pain; fibromyalgia/chronic widespread pain; autoimmune pain context

unitMap.text: Cancer pain and palliative interfaces
coveredTopics: Cancer-related pain mechanisms; bone pain; treatment-related neuropathy; opioid/nonopioid concepts; palliative/hospice coordination; intrathecal/neurolytic concepts

unitMap.text: Neuromodulation, targeted drug delivery, and device safety
coveredTopics: SCS/PNS concepts; implanted devices; targeted drug delivery; candidacy, trial response, contraindications; device labeling; adverse events

unitMap.text: Special populations, ethics, systems, and synthesis
coveredTopics: Pediatric, geriatric, pregnancy, renal/hepatic impairment; sickle cell disease; trauma/PTSD; ethics; privacy; disability; QI; coordination

topicGaps: No public lecture set found that can replace supervised technical performance, fluoroscopy/ultrasound skills, sedation, complication management, operating-room airway experience, or longitudinal patient care.

The ready ledger is rich in chronic-pain biopsychosocial content but thinner in structured, fellowship-level procedure safety, acute/postoperative, cancer/palliative, and board-specific evidence-appraisal instruction; the linked Stanford CME additions and planned original clips address concepts only.
Public Johns Hopkins material does not disclose a complete didactic timetable, exact lecture durations, case/procedure log, individual performance assessment, or full rotation calendar.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Anesthesiology (ABA) — Pain Medicine
American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR) — Pain Medicine
American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) — Pain Medicine
medical.boardStatus: Pain Medicine is a multidisciplinary subspecialty certification jointly recognized by ABA, ABPMR, and ABPN. The ABA administers the shared computer-based examination; each participating board controls its own applicant eligibility and certificate. The public ABA blueprint states 200 single-best-answer questions over four hours, divided 50% General and 50% Clinical States.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Completion of this independent course, watching videos, passing its original questions, or completing any planned clip does NOT establish or preserve eligibility, board certification, licensure, clinical privileges, DEA/CDS authority, ACGME credit, fellowship completion, case/procedure volume, or eligibility for any board exam. Johns Hopkins itself says successful completion of its ACGME fellowship does not by itself confer subspecialty certification; applicants must independently meet their primary board’s requirements. Exact published examples: ABPMR requires its diplomate in good standing, a current valid unrestricted U.S./territory/Canada license, 12 months of qualifying ACGME pain fellowship, and program-director recommendation. ABPN requires certification in neurology, child neurology, or psychiatry by December 31 of the preceding year and 12 months ACGME pain training completed by July 31 of the exam year; it currently does not accept international program training. The ABA exam page/blueprint must be consulted for ABA-specific current rules. Requirements, dates, and pathways change; verify directly with the intended board before relying on any plan.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Pain Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Actual, named one-year multidisciplinary ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship—not a generic directory category. The public page reports continuous ACGME accreditation since 1994, six annual fellows, NRMP positions, and collaboration between Anesthesiology & Critical Care Medicine and Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. Publicly described clinical exposure includes outpatient/inpatient consultation, chronic nonmalignant, cancer, and pediatric pain at the Blaustein Pain Treatment Center; rotations of 1–2 weeks in Anesthesiology, Neurology/Neurosurgery, Palliative Care, PM&R, and Psychiatry; and weekly lectures, oncology/spine conferences, grand rounds, journal clubs, and multidisciplinary pain conferences. It also describes a separate optional T32 research partnership. Public page descriptions are not a complete rotation schedule, case log, or a transcript of lectures.

officialProgrammes.name: Mass General Brigham Integrated Pain Medicine Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This record is an actual separate Johns Hopkins clinical physician fellowship, not a directory category. Study scope is a transparent independent, board-blueprint-aligned review of publicly described pain-medicine knowledge. It does not reproduce or claim access to Hopkins’ internal didactics, proprietary cases, clinical log, rotation schedule, supervision, or assessment. The user outline concerned nuclear medicine/radiology; it is out of scope for MED-014 and supplied no support for pain medicine, so none of its claims were adopted.
sourceCaveats: Webpage and video availability, board dates/fees, program leadership, regulations, device labeling, and guidelines can change. URLs were read/checked on 2026-10-07; consult the live primary source before relying on a claim.

YouTube duration metadata establishes public recording length at observation, not the quality, completeness, currency, curricular equivalence, or CME status of a lecture. The 68 Stanford playlist lectures are explicitly pain-focused but several cover related biopsychosocial subtopics from different speakers; every ID is counted once and no playlist is replayed for hours.

The public Johns Hopkins page is a programme description. It does not expose a complete internal syllabus, patient/case logs, protected case conferences, competency decisions, or individual assessments. Clinical rotations are reported as clinical exposure and never counted as video lectures.

The ABA blueprint is a public exam specification, not proprietary questions. All practice questions here are newly written educational items; they are not official questions, recalled items, or a predictive exam bank.

Guidelines and FDA pages define limited scopes and product contexts. They must not be used as individualized treatment orders. No dose, taper, injection approach, implant setting, or clinical decision is supplied.

Open-i/MedPix availability and licensing are item-specific. This course contains only links and licensing instructions, not copied images, real records, proprietary images, or synthetic “patient” scans.

topicGaps: No public lecture set found that can replace supervised technical performance, fluoroscopy/ultrasound skills, sedation, complication management, operating-room airway experience, or longitudinal patient care.

The ready ledger is rich in chronic-pain biopsychosocial content but thinner in structured, fellowship-level procedure safety, acute/postoperative, cancer/palliative, and board-specific evidence-appraisal instruction; the linked Stanford CME additions and planned original clips address concepts only.
Public Johns Hopkins material does not disclose a complete didactic timetable, exact lecture durations, case/procedure log, individual performance assessment, or full rotation calendar.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient says, “My pain is real even though the scan did not explain it.” Which statement best reflects the current IASP terminology?

options.text: Pain can be inferred only from nociceptor activity.
Pain is a personal sensory and emotional experience; pain and nociception are different phenomena.
Pain requires visible tissue damage.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IASP states that pain is personal and that pain and nociception are different phenomena; an imaging result alone cannot validate or invalidate the report.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description best matches NICE’s scope for chronic primary pain?

options.text: Pain lasting more than 3 months always caused by structural disease.
Pain with no clear underlying cause, or pain/impact out of proportion to observable injury or disease.
Any pain that has not responded to an injection.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE defines chronic primary pain in those terms and distinguishes it from chronic secondary pain; the guideline addresses assessment of all chronic pain and management of chronic primary pain.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional outpatient with acute musculoskeletal pain asks for an opioid. Which is the most accurate CDC 2022 framing?

options.text: Opioids are required before nonopioid options are tried.
Nonopioid therapies are at least as effective as opioids for many common acute pain conditions; consider opioid therapy only when benefits are anticipated to outweigh risks.
CDC recommendations are mandatory dosage limits for every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends maximizing appropriate nonpharmacologic and nonopioid pharmacologic therapies for many common acute pain conditions and emphasizes its recommendations are voluntary, not inflexible standards. Cancer/palliative/end-of-life pain are outside its scope.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional older adult with COPD uses an opioid and is being considered for pregabalin. What specific FDA safety issue must be recognized?

options.text: Gabapentinoids have no interaction concern with opioids.
Respiratory risk factors, including opioids/CNS depressants, COPD, and older age, can increase risk of serious breathing difficulties.
Pregabalin can be started without monitoring when used for nerve pain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA warns of serious breathing difficulties with gabapentin/pregabalin in people with respiratory risk factors and advises low-dose initiation and monitoring when co-prescribed with opioids or other CNS depressants. This is a safety concept, not a prescription instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which experience does the ACGME FAQ state cannot be fully substituted by a simulator/mannequin for pain medicine fellows who need anesthesiology experience?

options.text: Direct operating-room experience with laryngeal mask airway and/or endotracheal intubation backup.
A journal club presentation.
Reviewing a public pain lecture.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACGME FAQ says pain medicine fellows must gain this anesthesiology experience through direct patient care in the operating-room environment; a simulator/mannequin is not acceptable for all or part. This underscores why this independent curriculum cannot replace fellowship training.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is explicitly listed among ACGME pain medicine interventional treatment competencies?

options.text: Sympathetic blocks.
Independent unsupervised device implantation after watching a lecture.
Replacing a full neurologic history with imaging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACGME list includes epidural injections, trigger point injections, facet/medial branch blocks, neuroablative procedures, joint/bursa injections, sympathetic blocks, and peripheral nerve blocks. Competence requires supervised hands-on clinical training, not this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: For ABPMR Pain Medicine subspecialty certification, which combination is required in addition to the exam application?

options.text: Any medical license and a self-study completion certificate.
ABPMR diplomate in good standing, current valid unrestricted U.S./territory/Canada license, 12 months of qualifying ACGME pain fellowship, and program-director recommendation.
Completion of any one-year clinical observership.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPMR specifies these board-specific requirements; the fellowship must be completed by the stated pre-exam deadline. This independent course cannot confer any of them.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the ABPN Pain Medicine pathway published for its diplomates?

options.text: Any physician completing a pain lecture series can apply.
Applicants must be ABPN-certified in neurology, child neurology, or psychiatry by December 31 of the preceding year and complete 12 months of ACGME pain training by July 31 of the exam year.
International pain training is automatically accepted.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN lists those specific requirements and says it currently does not accept international program training. The ABA administers the shared examination; eligibility remains board-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: On the ABA Pain Medicine Exam blueprint, which major content category accounts for half of the examination?

options.text: General only.
Clinical States only.
Both General and Clinical States, each 50%.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The public blueprint assigns General 50% and Clinical States 50%. It lists pharmacotherapy and procedural treatment as 15% each within General. This original item is not an ABA exam question.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner sees an FDA page for the Evoke SCS System. Which conclusion is warranted?

options.text: Every person with chronic pain is an SCS candidate.

The device-specific page describes an aid for chronic intractable trunk/limb pain and lists, among other limits, inability to operate the system, ineffective trial stimulation, and poor surgical candidacy as reasons it should not be used.
The page authorizes independent implantation by a learner.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA’s page is device-specific and includes stated indications and “should not be used” conditions. It is not a universal indication, treatment recommendation, credential, or procedural authorization.

title: Regional Anesthesiology and Acute Pain Medicine Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship — independent-study curriculum only; not an affiliation, fellowship, residency, or credential-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Completed or current accredited anesthesiology residency-level knowledge is the intended clinical level; JHU and ACGME describe anesthesiology residency as the entry field for the fellowship.
Working knowledge of perioperative physiology, sterile technique, airway/resuscitation systems, pharmacology, ultrasound fundamentals, consent, and clinical documentation.
This study requires no patient contact and does not authorize needle insertion, local-anesthetic administration, medication adjustment, interpretation for care, or independent clinical decisions.
objectives: Apply a safety-first, source-aware framework to regional and acute-pain questions.
Interpret functional anatomy and ultrasound teaching material while recognizing uncertainty and supervision limits.

Use current ASRA safety sources for learning, while recognizing that local policy and qualified judgment govern clinical care.
Distinguish ACGME RAAPM training requirements from ABA Pain Medicine certification and from independent self-study.
Critically appraise authentic, de-identified, licensed case literature without rehosting or treating it as universal guidance.

topicGaps: No verified 36-hour free public lecture corpus was found: the updated unique observed-duration ledger totals 20.615000 hours, leaving 15.385000 hours below the target. The ASRA source adds meaningful open lectures, but its catalogue remains a curated subset, not a complete fellowship curriculum.

Insufficient public instruction remains for longitudinal supervised clinical reasoning, formal acute-pain-service workflow and handoffs, institution-specific protocols, current guideline application across every drug/procedure/population, complete pediatric and trauma experiences, complication simulation, and observed/assessed technical performance. Video cannot substitute for these experiences.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

The ASRA source adds meaningful open lectures, but its catalogue remains a curated subset, not a complete fellowship curriculum.

Insufficient public instruction remains for longitudinal supervised clinical reasoning, formal acute-pain-service workflow and handoffs, institution-specific protocols, current guideline application across every drug/procedure/population, complete pediatric and trauma experiences, complication simulation, and observed/assessed technical performance. practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wants a current source for regional-anesthesia decisions in a patient receiving an antithrombotic medicine. Which is the best starting source in this course?

options.text: ASRA fifth-edition regional-anesthesia antithrombotic guideline
An undated technique video
A general social-media post
A local protocol from an unknown institution

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ASRA fifth edition is the dated specialty guidance in the course. Its recommendations still require drug-, procedure-, and local-policy-specific interpretation by qualified clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a fictional post-injection simulation, a patient develops concerning neurologic and cardiovascular symptoms. What is the best immediate educational priority?

options.text: Use the institution’s emergency response and LAST checklist; call for help
Continue the planned teaching session
Wait for symptoms to resolve before alerting anyone
Rely on an online video rather than local emergency resources

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASRA frames LAST as rare but life-threatening and its checklist begins with rapid emergency preparedness. This question deliberately does not teach medication doses.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ACGME RAAPM minimum is correctly paired with its experience category?

options.text: 100 upper-extremity nerve block procedures
20 total nerve block procedures across all sites
No truncal-block experience is required
Five months of chronic pain only

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 RAAPM requirements specify at least 100 upper-extremity nerve block procedures and separately define lower-extremity, truncal, neuraxial, catheter, and pain-service experiences. These are accredited-training requirements, not independent-study targets.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the ACGME RAAPM standard require for acute-pain experience?

options.text: At least three months, including supervised inpatient assessment/management and 50 unique documented new patients
A single acute-pain lecture
Only operating-room observation
No acute-pain experience

practiceQuestions.rationale: The requirements specify at least three months of acute-pain experience and 50 unique documented new patients. Watching recorded lectures does not satisfy this clinical requirement.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes RAAPM fellowship from Pain Medicine subspecialty certification?

options.text: The ABA list includes Pain Medicine but does not list RAAPM as a separate ABA subspecialty exam
RAAPM fellowship automatically confers ABA Pain Medicine certification
Any self-study course creates Pain Medicine exam eligibility
All pain-related fellowships have the same board pathway

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA’s current subspecialty list names Pain Medicine but not RAAPM. The course makes no certification or eligibility claim.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional shoulder-surgery discussion, why is a generic block video insufficient to choose an approach?

options.text: Approach selection depends on surgical distribution, patient-specific risk, alternatives, supervision, and local practice
The most-viewed video determines the safest technique
A learner can infer consent from the planned surgery
Respiratory and neurologic history are unrelated to planning

practiceQuestions.rationale: JHU’s objectives include appropriate patient selection, consent, and recognition/management of complications. Videos are education, not patient-specific decision authority.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source best supports an educational review of infection-control considerations for regional anesthesia and pain procedures?

options.text: ASRA Pain Medicine 2025 infection-control guideline
A technique thumbnail with no clinical policy
A course participant’s recollection
An unrelated imaging guideline

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASRA’s 2025 guideline specifically addresses infection prevention across regional anesthesia and pain procedures, including ultrasound-specific recommendations.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which RAAPM exposure is explicitly required in the ACGME standard in addition to regional and acute-pain experience?

options.text: Pediatric experience and trauma experience
A radiology residency rotation
A nuclear medicine board examination
No non-OR experience

practiceQuestions.rationale: The RAAPM requirements explicitly require pediatric and trauma experience. The unrelated nuclear-medicine material in the supplied user outline does not belong to this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner uses the linked 2026 Frontiers LAST case report. Which is the most accurate use?

options.text: Critically discuss recognition, communication, and limits of one case while citing its CC BY source
Treat one case as a universal dosing protocol
Remove patient-consent context and rehost any material without attribution
Claim the case establishes independent procedural competence

practiceQuestions.rationale: The report is CC BY and states patient consent; it is useful for source-linked discussion, not a universal protocol or competence credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct role of the 36-hour target in this course?

options.text: A curriculum-floor target combining ready recordings and clearly labeled planned original production; it is not clinical-training time
Proof of fellowship completion
A substitute for procedure logs
A guarantee of board eligibility or passing

practiceQuestions.rationale: Only the observed-duration public recordings in the ledger are ready. The exact remainder is planned production and is not counted as completed video or clinical training.

title: Adult Cardiothoracic Anesthesiology
prerequisites: For appropriate level-setting only: completed or near-completed accredited anesthesiology residency-level foundations in airway management, general anesthesia, invasive monitoring, resuscitation, pharmacology, and critical care. This is not an admission rule or proof of fellowship eligibility.
Working knowledge of adult cardiac anatomy, ECG, ventilator physiology, hemodynamics, anticoagulation principles, transthoracic echo terminology, and sterile/procedural safety concepts.

Access to local supervised clinical governance and credentialed teaching for any patient-facing task. Do not insert a TEE probe, manage CPB/MCS, set anticoagulation, prescribe, or make treatment decisions based on this independent material.
objectives: Construct a perioperative problem representation for adult cardiac, aortic, structural, electrophysiology, and noncardiac thoracic procedures.
Interpret, at a conceptual level, hemodynamic traces and perioperative echo images while naming uncertainty, artefact, and the escalation path to a credentialed supervisor.
Explain CPB phases, organ-protection considerations, and bleeding/thrombosis decision frames without substituting a local protocol.
Compare physiologic goals and perioperative hazards across coronary, ventricular, valvular, adult-congenital, aortic, and mechanical-support presentations.
Use current guideline and programme sources to communicate a structured multidisciplinary plan, postoperative handoff, and evidence uncertainty.
Practice original single-best-answer reasoning aligned transparently to the public 2025 ABA ACA blueprint, not to recalled or proprietary examination material.

units.title: Foundations, scope, and adult cardiovascular physiology
objectives: Relate the ACTA fellowship name to ABA ACA certification without conflating them.
Explain pressure-flow, oxygen-delivery, ventricular interaction, and coronary-perfusion concepts used in later units.
boardDomains: A. Foundations of Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology (5%)
units.casePractice: No patient-facing practice. Create a physiology concept map from a fictional low-output vignette, then list information that is missing before any decision could be made.
units.assessment: 10-item formative retrieval quiz and a 250-word uncertainty-aware physiology explanation.

units.title: Preoperative evaluation and multidisciplinary planning
objectives: Organize a preoperative assessment around procedure, ventricular/valve disease, ischemic risk, pulmonary status, frailty, antithrombotic context, and available data.
Separate educational risk framing from clinical recommendation or clearance.
boardDomains: B. Preoperative Evaluation of the Patient for Cardiac Surgery (7%)
units.casePractice: Use the linked aortic-stenosis case in hidden-diagnosis mode; inventory data, limitations, and which specialist inputs a fictional preoperative conference would require.
units.assessment: Structured fictional-case preoperative template; peer/self-check against a supplied rubric.

units.title: Monitoring, TEE foundations, and echo interpretation limits
objectives: Describe indications, information yield, contraindication/complication awareness, and limits of perioperative TEE conceptually.
Recognize why image quality, acquisition plane, Doppler alignment, and context condition an interpretation.
units.casePractice: Annotate a linked, de-identified image stack only in the web source: view name, visible structures, quality limitation, and question for a credentialed interpreter. Do not download or redistribute images.
units.assessment: Twenty-label image-orientation exercise using nonpatient conceptual diagrams plus a limitation statement for each.

units.title: Cardiopulmonary bypass, anticoagulation concepts, and organ protection
objectives: Describe the components and phases of CPB and the anesthesiologist–perfusionist shared situational-awareness model.
Explain why CPB requires contextual monitoring of perfusion, temperature, acid-base strategy, coagulation, cerebral/renal risk, and communication.
units.casePractice: Tabletop only: make a fictional ‘before CPB / on CPB / separation’ communication checklist. Do not use it as a clinical protocol.
units.assessment: Scenario-based sequencing quiz and a one-page systems-safety debrief.

units.title: Mechanical circulatory support, transplant, and advanced heart failure
objectives: Contrast the physiologic purpose and major monitoring questions of temporary support, durable VAD, and transplant contexts.
Identify when a learner must defer to local device expertise and formal institutional protocols.
units.casePractice: Fictional MCS handoff analysis: distinguish observed data, inferred physiology, and items requiring device-team confirmation.
units.assessment: Short-answer concept map and two original single-best-answer questions.

units.title: Coronary disease, ventricular dysfunction, and ischemia
objectives: Link coronary anatomy, ventricular function, loading conditions, and ischemia monitoring to a perioperative reasoning framework.
Describe what a new wall-motion finding can and cannot establish without expert confirmation.
units.casePractice: Fictional post-bypass low-output reasoning map: identify differential categories and which data should be checked, without choosing treatment.
units.assessment: Original vignette quiz with a mandatory ‘what would change my confidence?’ response.

units.title: Valvular and structural heart disease
objectives: Use a mechanism-first vocabulary for aortic, mitral, tricuspid, and prosthetic valve disease.
Recognize the distinct roles of TEE, procedural imaging, and the multidisciplinary valve team.
units.casePractice: Linked de-identified aortic-stenosis case: write an image-quality note and identify why a complete formal echo/valve-team interpretation remains necessary.
units.assessment: Valve-mechanism matching exercise and brief source-cited case reflection.

units.title: Adult congenital disease and structural interventions
objectives: Identify why repaired congenital anatomy requires lesion-specific anatomy, shunt, ventricular, rhythm, and access planning.
Differentiate adult congenital exposure in ACTA from the separate pediatric cardiac anesthesia fellowship.
units.casePractice: Fictional repaired-congenital anatomy worksheet; flag the missing operative history and need for ACHD consultation.
units.assessment: Diagram-labeling and one escalation-focused written response.

units.title: Thoracic aortic and noncardiac thoracic anesthesia
objectives: Explain the anesthetic relevance of aortic pathology, cerebral/spinal-cord protection concepts, imaging, and multidisciplinary aortic-team coordination.
Outline one-lung ventilation and thoracic surgical concerns at a conceptual—not procedural—level.
units.casePractice: Linked Type-B dissection echo case in hidden-diagnosis mode: classify the image finding and list imaging/report limitations; no management plan or patient-specific advice.
units.assessment: Aortic-imaging terminology quiz and fictional team-briefing checklist.

units.title: Electrophysiology and rhythm procedures
objectives: Recognize procedure-specific anesthetic, anticoagulation, airway, access, and TEE information questions in EP work.
Describe rhythm–hemodynamic interactions and the importance of local device/EP protocols.
units.casePractice: Fictional EP procedure time-out: state who owns anticoagulation/device decisions and which local protocol must be consulted.
units.assessment: Single-best-answer question set plus a nontechnical-skills checklist.

units.title: Postoperative cardiac surgical critical care and handoff
objectives: Organize a structured post-CPB/postoperative handoff around procedure, support, hemostasis, ventilation, hemodynamics, echo findings, and uncertainties.
Differentiate educational reasoning from ICU orders or independent critical-care practice.
units.casePractice: Fictional ICU handoff using a structured template; explicitly label observations versus pending verification.
units.assessment: Faculty-independent self-audit against the handoff rubric and short-answer safety quiz.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, ethics, quality improvement, and blueprint integration
objectives: Map study time to the public ABA blueprint without claiming it reproduces the exam.
Appraise guideline scope, study-date, applicability, and uncertainty; communicate limitations and escalation.
topics: ACGME versus board versus NBE boundaries
boardDomains: All ACA blueprint domains; especially L. Other Topics (4%)
units.casePractice: Prepare a source-cited, de-identified linked-case discussion using only facts displayed by the source; do not copy images or create a real-patient record.
units.assessment: Capstone written case conference, 40-item original formative quiz, and evidence-appraisal checklist.

assignment.title: Independent ACTA evidence-and-case portfolio
deliverables: A blueprint map that assigns each of the 12 public ABA domains to one unit and at least one current source.
Two linked-case reflections using the licensed/de-identified web cases; include modality, visible findings, limitations, source citation, and an escalation statement. Do not download/rehost images.
One fictional, nonpatient CPB or postoperative handoff communication plan that cites the 2024 CPB guideline and labels itself nonclinical.
A 750–1,000 word critique of one current guideline’s scope, date, recommendations versus local protocol, and uncertainty.
assignment.submissionStandard: No real patient data, screenshots, proprietary board items, hospital protocols, or treatment advice. This is an educational portfolio, not a clinical case log.

formative: Original vignette reasoning with explicit uncertainty
assessment.summativePlan: Capstone portfolio (40%), original 40-item single-best-answer formative exam (35%), source-appraisal note (15%), and safety/limits reflection (10%). A suggested 80% threshold is only a study milestone, not a certification, credentialing, or passing prediction.
assessment.academicIntegrity: All questions below are original educational items. No ABA, NBE, ACGME, SCA, institutional, or recalled examination content is reproduced.

medical.boardStatus: This is an actual ACGME subspecialty fellowship, not a generic directory category. ACGME uses the name Adult Cardiothoracic Anesthesiology (ACTA); ABA’s distinct ABMS subspecialty certificate/exam is named Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology (ACA). NBE Advanced PTE is separate from ABA ACA certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not confer a fellowship, case log, clinical competence, ABA/NBE eligibility, certification, licensure, hospital privileges, or a passing result. Current ABA registration requires an unrestricted US/Canadian license, at least one ABA certification, MOCA participation, current privileges and adult cardiac clinical activity averaging at least one day/week for 12 consecutive months in the preceding three years, and ability to practice the full scope with or without reasonable accommodation. The ABA permanent ACA pathway also specifies completion of an ACGME CTA fellowship plus current NBE Advanced PTE certification, or recent-fellow/testamur conditions stated by ABA. Temporary pathways for certain non-ACGME or shorter fellowship/practice histories are explicitly limited to 2023–2028 and require current Advanced PTE certification or testamur status plus the stated practice criteria; do not infer eligibility from this course. The NBE Advanced PTEeXAM is an examination of advanced perioperative TEE, not an ABA certificate and not a substitute for supervised training.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Study scope is adult perioperative cardiac and cardiothoracic anesthesiology: preoperative assessment; invasive monitoring; CPB; mechanical support; cardiac/valvular/aortic/selected adult congenital disease; electrophysiology/structural procedures; postoperative critical care; and noncardiac thoracic anesthesia. It deliberately distinguishes the adult fellowship from Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesiology and from Anesthesiology Critical Care Medicine, although each can overlap clinically. It does not claim the Hopkins programme’s cases, faculty, protected teaching, TEE simulator, conferences, rotations, supervision, or pass-rate as course assets.
sourceCaveats: Sources were read on 2026-10-07. Guidelines and eligibility can change; current board and local policy govern any real application.

The Hopkins public page describes an actual programme but does not publish a complete reusable lecture library or individual clinical experience; no institutional material is represented as course-owned.
The video ledger counts only public watch-page runtimes observed on the stated date. Public playback is not permission to copy, download, embed, crop, or rehost.
Only 6.5075 hours of ready observed video were found; 29.4925 hours remain unavailable. Planned clips are not films and add zero verified hours.

Radiopaedia cases are linked, not copied. Public cases display de-identified metadata but the course cannot independently validate original consent/de-identification process; users must comply with Radiopaedia’s noncommercial attribution terms and current site guidance.
No free, current, lawfully reusable full cardiothoracic-anesthesia textbook was verified. The reading list prioritizes official PDFs and guideline pages; it is not a textbook substitute.
This work corrects the irrelevant nuclear-medicine/radiology outline by excluding it from the ACTA course; no radiology/theranostics claims are imported.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional exam blueprint review asks which content category has the greatest relative weight in the ABA Adult Cardiac Anesthesiology blueprint. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Preoperative evaluation, 7%
Management of CPB, 15%
Adult congenital heart disease, 15%
Postoperative considerations, 15%

practiceQuestions.rationale: The April 2025 blueprint assigns 15% each to CPB, cardiac diseases, and valvular heart disease. Preoperative evaluation is 7%, adult congenital disease 4%, and postoperative considerations 5%.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional learning exercise, a trainee says that a published 12-month fellowship rotation schedule can be counted as 12 months of video lecture time. What is the best correction?

options.text: Yes, any supervised clinical month equals 36 video hours.
Yes, because ACGME requires didactics.
No; supervised clinical experiences and rotations are not lecture recordings and cannot be counted as video hours.
No, because fellowship contains no didactics.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requires a blend of supervised patient care, clinical teaching, and didactic events, while the Hopkins page lists rotations. Neither converts clinical time into observed video runtime.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional on-pump case conference asks which item is explicitly included in the ACGME minimum cardiac-experience requirement for ACTA fellows. Which is correct?

options.text: At least 100 cardiac surgical procedures, with at least 50 requiring CPB
At least 100 independent TEE examinations
At least 50 lung transplants
At least 100 hours of recorded CPB lectures

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACGME document specifies a minimum 100 cardiac surgical procedures, at least 50 requiring CPB, within at least six months of clinical anesthesia. These are supervised clinical requirements, not video or independent-practice requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional perioperative echo learner obtains one technically limited view and proposes to use it alone to rule out all important pathology. What is the best response?

options.text: One view is sufficient if the learner is confident.
A limited image must be interpreted with acquisition quality, clinical context, additional views/data, and credentialed supervision; it may not answer every question.
Only 3D images need contextual interpretation.
The NBE exam authorizes independent clinical interpretation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NBE page defines an examination/certification pathway, not autonomous clinical authority. Safe educational interpretation requires recognizing image limitations and escalation; this course does not teach independent probe use or diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with a mechanical prosthetic valve also has atrial fibrillation. Which statement matches the 2020 ACC/AHA guideline summary?

options.text: A NOAC is recommended instead of a VKA in every mechanical prosthesis.
A NOAC should not be used in a patient with a mechanical prosthesis, with or without atrial fibrillation.
Anticoagulation has no relevance to a mechanical prosthesis.
The source establishes a perioperative dosing protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACC summary states that a NOAC should not be used in patients with a mechanical prosthesis, with or without AF. This item tests the published boundary only; it does not supply perioperative management or dosing advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A linked de-identified educational case shows an intimal flap distal to the left subclavian artery and the case discussion labels the condition Stanford type B. What is the most appropriate study action?

options.text: Use the linked case to practice labeling the finding and document image/source limits.
Download the images and add them to a new proprietary question bank without attribution.
Treat the web case as a patient-specific management order set.
Call it a synthetic teaching image.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Radiopaedia case is an authentic, publicly linked educational resource with case data and discussion. The lawful course use is linked viewing/attribution-aware study, not unlicensed rehosting or patient-specific management.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional MCS discussion states that a durable-device guideline addresses only LVAD implantation and not biventricular support. Which correction is supported by the ISHLT source?

options.text: The guideline is limited to pediatric ECMO.
The 2023 update also covers all configurations of durable MCS, including single and biventricular support.
The guideline contains no intraoperative content.
The guideline grants device-operating privileges.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ISHLT states that the update covers durable MCS configurations including single and biventricular support and includes intraoperative/immediate postoperative management task forces. It does not grant privileges or replace device-team training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional curriculum designer calls an Adult Cardiothoracic Anesthesiology fellowship a Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesiology fellowship because both involve congenital disease. What is the best correction?

options.text: They are identical because all congenital disease is pediatric.
ACTA is an adult fellowship; its required cardiac experience may include adult correction/revision of congenital lesions, while Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesiology is separately listed by ACGME.
Neither specialty involves congenital anatomy.
A lecture series determines fellowship identity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME lists Adult Cardiothoracic Anesthesiology and Pediatric Cardiac Anesthesiology separately. ACTA requirements include adult correction/revision of congenital lesions as one possible category, which does not merge the fellowships.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional applicant has completed an ACGME CTA fellowship and passed the Advanced PTEeXAM but has not yet completed NBE certification documentation. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The self-study course itself supplies ACA eligibility.

ABA’s published permanent and temporary criteria distinguish current NBE Advanced PTE certification from testamur/recent-fellow conditions; the applicant must verify the current pathway directly with ABA.
NBE and ABA are the same organization.
No license or ABA certification is needed to register.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA’s eligibility PDF contains pathway-specific NBE certification/testamur wording, while its registration page adds license, ABA certification, MOCA, privilege, and practice requirements. Eligibility is individual and must be confirmed with ABA.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner totals eight distinct observed public videos at 23,427 seconds. What is the correct transparent report against a 36-hour target?

options.text: 36 hours verified because rotations and readings can fill the remainder.
6.5075 verified video hours and a 29.4925-hour gap; planned clips do not count until rendered, duration-probed, and publicly accessible.
23,427 hours verified because seconds do not need conversion.
Count the same playlist entries twice to reach the floor.

practiceQuestions.rationale: 23,427 / 3,600 = 6.5075 hours. The exact difference from 36 is 29.4925 hours. This course never counts planned clips, readings, rotations, or duplicate IDs as ready video.

boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Adult Congenital Heart Disease Certification

boardStatus.status: This is a distinct clinical physician fellowship specialty, not a generic directory category. ABIM administers a distinct Adult Congenital Heart Disease Certification Examination; the fellowship itself does not confer a separate institution-issued board credential.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: January 2026 ABIM CERT: Embryology/Anatomy 4%; Clinical Evaluation 10%; Noninvasive Testing 20%; Cath 7%; Arrhythmias 15%; Surgery 12%; HF/PH 10%; Reproductive 5%; Acquired Adult Problems 5%; Extracardiac 7%; Life/Health Management 5%. Content specification only; no proprietary items or guarantee.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent self-study does not establish ABIM eligibility, accredited-fellowship completion, clinical competence, unrestricted licensure, procedure experience, credentialing, ABIM/ABP certification, or exam success. Per ABIM policy checked 2026-10-07, certification requires prior ABIM cardiovascular-disease or ABP pediatric-cardiology certification at application, qualifying formal training or any applicable practice-pathway experience, documented competence/ethics, unrestricted/unencumbered licence, and passing the examination. The Training Pathway requires 24 ACHD months including 18 clinical months; training begun on/after 2019-07-01 must be ACGME/RCPSC/CMQ accredited/recognized. Training must be complete by October 31 of the exam year and cannot be double-counted. Policies can change; ABIM alone decides individual eligibility.
